title: How freight brokers reach the right shipper decision-maker.
seoTitle: How freight brokers reach the right shipper decision-maker
searchIntent: How can freight brokers reach logistics decision-makers?
excerpt: Approach reception with context, identify who controls freight, and use truthful internal introductions to find the right contact.
takeaway: Make it easy for someone to route a relevant inquiry. A different contact path should clarify responsibility, not disguise your purpose.

sections.title: Understand why the call is being screened.
paragraphs: Reception and customer-service staff are protecting coworkers’ time as well as directing calls. Luis’s gatekeeper lessons begin with that reality. A stranger asking for someone important without explaining the relevance of the call gives the person answering little reason to help.

Approach the interaction as a routing problem. You need to find the person who can discuss a particular business need. That is different from treating the employee as an obstacle to defeat. A respectful, concise exchange is more useful than a long sales introduction before you know whether you are speaking to the right person.

sections.title: Use a real fact to establish relevance.
paragraphs: Luis describes confirming a simple fact about the company’s product or location before requesting the appropriate contact. The source examples include corn production and plastic bags. The purpose is to connect the inquiry to the company’s actual work.

Only use information you have verified. If you mention experience with a product or customer, it must be experience you actually have. Sounding familiar should not involve pretending that you already have a relationship, a pending shipment, or a conversation that never occurred.

sections.title: Ask for the person who owns the decision.
paragraphs: Knowing a name can make routing easier, but a title does not always establish purchasing authority. Logistics, purchasing, operations, and management can share different parts of the transportation process. Your objective is to learn who handles the particular need you are discussing.

Luis recommends short, plain requests rather than elaborate greetings. After establishing relevance, ask to be connected with the person responsible. If the answer identifies another role or location, that is useful research. Record it so the next attempt uses the information you just received.

sections.title: Change the route when the current one is not working.
paragraphs: Repeatedly making the same unanswered request does not necessarily improve your position. The lesson discusses using other legitimate paths, including purchasing, sales, customer service, or professional-profile research, to understand how the organization is arranged.

A second lesson adds the possibility of a senior introduction. An owner, purchasing leader, or executive may direct the inquiry to the correct employee. The purpose of that contact can be brief routing rather than a complete sales pitch to a person who does not manage daily freight.

sections.title: Keep a senior introduction truthful and limited.
paragraphs: Luis uses his experience with a family manufacturing company to explain why different people may respond differently to incoming calls. An owner may be reachable when a routine vendor channel is heavily screened. That is an observation from the lesson, not a rule that all owners answer or welcome every solicitation.

If a senior person directs you to a colleague, represent that introduction accurately. Being told whom to call is not the same as being endorsed as an approved provider. The distinction protects the credibility of the next conversation.

sections.title: Check whether the target fits your business.
paragraphs: Persistent access problems can also prompt a review of the prospect itself. Luis notes that smaller or midsize organizations can have more direct contact paths than a large corporate purchasing structure. This is a targeting consideration, not a guarantee that smaller customers are easier to win.

Decide whether the expected opportunity justifies the effort and whether another prospect is a better fit. Respect explicit refusals. Effective prospecting involves choosing where to invest attention, not proving that every closed route can eventually be forced open.
